extracted.intended_audience: authors, critics, and general readers of literary satire (18th-century/contextual)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and descriptive observations about the behaviour, style, and moral responsibilities of authors, critics, and public men — advice on how to speak of others, how to criticize, and how writers should present themselves. Grounded in 18th-century satirical prose and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain the liberty of the press; avoid anonymous defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the liberty of the press, like every other privilege, it must be restrained within certain bounds; for if it is carried to a branch of law, religion, and charity, it becomes one of the greatest evils that ever annoyed the community. If the lowest ruffian may stab your good name with impunity in England, will you be so uncandid as to exclaim against Italy for the practice of common assassination?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page discusses consequences of anonymous libel (reputational ruin, difficulty proving damages before jury), countermeasures (prosecution ineffective; bringing action for damages requires proving specific harm), and extra-legal reprisals (physical assaults, bastinado) as historically practised. Anti-pattern: relying on a free press as permitting unchecked calumny; example anecdotes: a captain breaking a publisher’s bones after a newspaper slur; a low fellow bastinadoed in Lugano to stop his abuse. Also notes perverse fiscal incentive (stamp-duty revenue) that encourages toleration of scandalous press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to the mob; avoid flattering popular prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding my contempt for those who flatter a minister, I think there is something still more despicable in flattering a mob. When I see a man of birth, education, and fortune, put himself on a level with the dregs of the people ... flatter their prejudices, harangue in praise of their virtues ... I cannot help despising him, as a man guilty of the vilest prostitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive counsel discouraging authors/public figures from lowering themselves to win popular favour by pandering, mingling with vulgarity, or performing for crowds. Anti-pattern: sacrificing dignity and principle to gain popularity or votes; example behaviour: mingling with mechanics, adopting their manners and prejudices for selfish ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reasons and demonstration when you criticize; avoid dogmatic ipse dixit
rubrics_metrics.description: He took upon him to decide dogmatically upon every subject, without deigning to shew the least cause for his differing from the general opinions of mankind, as if it had been our duty to acquiesce in the ipse dixit of this new Pythagoras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgments should be supported by demonstration and argument. Anti-patterns: asserting conclusions without cause, sweeping condemnations of authors ('Milton was harsh and prosaic; Dryden, languid and verbose' etc.) and refusal to tolerate contradiction. Example: the narrator dissenting from such dogmatism because demonstration 'did not seem to be his talent.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain candour and modesty in discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: I would much rather see determined; whether the world was always as contemptible, as it appears to me at present?—If the morals of mankind have not contracted an extraordinary degree of depravity ... I should renounce politics the more willingly, if I could find other topics of conversation discussed with more modesty and candour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates for temperate, modest, and candid discourse rather than virulent factionalism. Anti-patterns: ‘virulent factions’ that revile and traduce one another; preference for measured conversation over zealotry and personal vitriol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let personal envy corrupt judgment; distinguish emulation from malice
rubrics_metrics.description: I am inclined to think, no mind was ever wholly exempt from envy; which, perhaps, may have been implanted, as an instinct essential to our nature. I am afraid we sometimes palliate this vice, under the spacious name of emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about envy: it can make a person uneasy when others are praised and corrupt honest appraisal. Anti-pattern: letting jealous uneasiness inform criticism or social behaviour; anecdote of a normally generous person showing unease when a friend is commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the image your writing creates; avoid appearing in public if your deportment contradicts your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Those originals are not fit for conversation. If they would maintain the advantage they have gained by their writing, they should never appear but upon paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author's personal manners and conversation undermine the qualities of their written work, they should avoid public appearances; the mismatch between written genius and illiberal personal conduct can destroy the impression of their art. Anti-pattern: an author whose sublime ideas are accompanied by illiberal sentiments in person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hominem invective, factional rancour and national invective in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: He damns all the other writers of the age, with the utmost insolence and rancour—One is a blunderbuss, as being a native of Ireland; another, a half-starved louse of literature, from the banks of the Tweed; a third, an ass, because he enjoys a pension from the government ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism grounded in personal attacks, national stereotyping, or factional abuse is portrayed as an anti-pattern. Good criticism should avoid name-calling, rancour, and attributing failure or vice to origin or patronage; examples show how pernicious and empty such attacks are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep debates focused and avoid pedantry that derails practical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: They launched out into tedious dissertations on the poetry of the ancients; and one of them, who had been a school-master, displayed his whole knowledge of prosody ... A confused hum of insipid observations and comments ensued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing specific literary questions (e.g., blank verse vs rhyme), avoid irrelevant appeals to ancient practice or excessive erudition that do not elucidate the modern question. Anti-pattern: a pedant who uses Greek and Latin quotations to obfuscate rather than clarify; example: discussion devolving into prosody gleaned from Disputer and Ruddiman rather than addressing the central issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value measured social gatherings: one strong wit is more productive than many competing ones
rubrics_metrics.description: My uncle says, he never desires to meet with more than one wit at a time—One wit, like a knuckle of ham in soup, gives a zest and flavour to the dish; but more than one serves only to spoil the pottage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance about social/critical gatherings: a single skilled conversationalist can enliven a group, whereas several competing wits spoil collective enjoyment. Anti-pattern: multiple strong voices clashing and dissipating the quality of conversation; metaphor and example provided.
